title: Why Dropshipping Won't Make You Rich (Even With Sales)

spine.goal: Dave wants to quit his job with an online store: sell a $30 glowing cat lamp he never touches, and clear $1,800 a month (his napkin math: $18 profit x 100 lamps).
spine.stakes: Every dollar comes from his savings and his credit card; one bad month costs him $1,546, and 'scaling up' would multiply it.
spine.central_question: Dave made $3,000 in sales. So where did the money go, and why is his bank account $1,546 lighter?
spine.loop_big: The one number Dave should have checked before spending a single dollar (his ad ceiling: about $16.80 per customer; he was paying $25). Promised in o6, paid in ch9.
spine.loop_mid: Pause-and-guess in ch3 (~30%): out of every 100 people who clicked Dave's ad, how many bought a lamp? Paid in ch4 (~40%): two.
spine.villain: Everyone who gets paid whether the store wins or loses: the ad platform (Meta: $59.4B ad revenue in Q2 2026, price per ad +12% y/y) and the store platform/payment processor (Shopify: $39 plan + 2.9% + 30c per sale; $2.78B merchant-solutions revenue in Q2 2026). Shovel sellers in a gold rush. Revealed in ch5 (~50%).
spine.low_point: ~75%: refunds, chargebacks and slow boats push the damage to $1,546, and Dave's thumb hovers over 'increase budget' to 'scale' a store that loses ~$8 on every sale.
spine.win: Dave turns off the ads and does the napkin math (education, not advice): search the product first ($9 elsewhere), test tiny with a stop rule ($50, not $500), read the bank account not the sales screen. He finds the ad ceiling ($16.80 < $25), closes the store and avoids month two: SAVED $1,546.

sources: Illustrative story (dramatized, not a real person's data): Dave's store, the glowing cat lamp, its $12 supplier cost (shipping included), $30 price, 50-cent clicks, 2-in-100 buy rate, 100 sales, 20 refunds and 2 chargebacks are example numbers chosen to show how the store math works; real stores vary widely

Shopify pricing page (shopify.com/pricing, checked Oct 2026): Basic plan $39 USD/month billed monthly ($29/month billed yearly); online credit card rate on Basic 2.9% + 30 cents (Shopify Payments, US)

Shopify Help Center, chargeback process (help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/chargebacks/chargeback-process, 2026): chargeback fee in the United States is $15 USD; if the merchant wins, the disputed amount and fee are returned, otherwise the merchant loses both

Shopify Help Center, Shopify Payments refunds (help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/payouts/refunds, 2026): the original credit card processing fee is not returned to the merchant when an order is refunded

Meta Platforms, 'Meta Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results' (investor.atmeta.com, July 2026): advertising revenue $59.363 billion in Q2 2026; ad impressions +14% year over year; average price per ad +12% year over year

Shopify Inc., Q2 2026 results press release (Form 8-K exhibit 99.1, SEC, August 5, 2026): merchant solutions revenue $2,781 million (mostly payments), subscription solutions revenue $802 million, total revenue $3,583 million, GMV $115.57 billion for the quarter ended June 30, 2026

U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Business Guide to the FTC's Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule' (ftc.gov): if a seller states no shipping time it must have a reasonable basis to ship within 30 days; if it can't ship on time it must get the buyer's consent to the delay or promptly refund all the money paid for unshipped merchandise

National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, '2025 Retail Returns Landscape' (NRF press release, Oct 15, 2025): retailers estimated 19.3% of online sales would be returned in 2025 (about 1 in 5); total returns $849.9 billion

Math (Dave's illustrative month): per lamp $30 - $12 supplier - $1.17 fee ($0.87 + $0.30) = $16.83 before ads (his 'ad ceiling'); 50 clicks x $0.50 = $25 of ads per sale, so -$8.17 per sale. Month: 100 x $30 = $3,000 sales; minus $1,200 lamps, $117 fees, $39 plan, $2,500 ads = -$856; minus 20 refunds x $30 = $600 -> -$1,456; minus 2 chargebacks x ($30 + $15 fee) = $90 -> -$1,546
Callbacks: episode 2 (raccoon toll booth = card swipe fee) and the classic 'sell shovels in a gold rush' saying (general business idiom, not a statistic)

beats.text: Dave's phone buzzes. Three thousand dollars in sales! Then he opens his bank app.
Yep. That's Dave. Rich on paper, broke in real life. Let's rewind.
A video promised Dave an easy store, run from his couch.
His real result? Minus one thousand five hundred forty six dollars.
So where did three thousand dollars go? Somebody got paid. Not Dave.
You'll see who. And the one number Dave should have checked first.
So Dave did exactly what the video said. He opened an online store on Shopify. Thirty nine dollars a month.
The trick is called dropshipping. Dave never touches a product. A customer buys on his website. Dave forwards the order to a supplier overseas. The supplier mails it straight to the customer.
Dave is basically a waiter who has never seen the kitchen. He takes your order, smiles, and hopes the food shows up.
His product? A glowing cat lamp. The supplier charges twelve dollars, shipping included. Dave sells it for thirty.
Eighteen dollars of profit per lamp! Dave grabbed a napkin. Sell a hundred lamps, make eighteen hundred dollars. Every month.
But Dave's napkin was missing a few lines. And the first one was hiding inside every single sale.
Then it happened. Dave's first sale. Thirty dollars! He took a screenshot and sent it to his mom.
But those thirty dollars never fully reached Dave. The payment fee came off first. Two point nine percent, plus thirty cents. About a dollar twenty.
Remember the raccoon toll booth from our credit card video? Every single sale drives through it. And the raccoon never misses one.
Then the supplier took its twelve dollars for the lamp. That leaves Dave about sixteen dollars and eighty cents.
Still not bad! Except for one small problem. Nobody knew Dave's store existed. Eight billion people on Earth, and one visitor a day. His mom.
So Dave did what every new store owner does. He paid for attention. And attention turned out to be the most expensive thing in the whole store.
Dave filmed a cute video of the lamp, and paid Facebook and Instagram to show it to strangers.
Every time somebody clicked, Dave paid about fifty cents. And people clicked! For the first time, Dave's store had visitors.
But a visitor is not a buyer. It's like handing out free cookie samples at the mall. Everybody takes one. Almost nobody buys the cookie jar.
Quick guess. Out of every hundred people who clicked Dave's ad, how many actually bought a lamp? Write your number in the comments. The answer is in a minute.
While you think, Dave kept paying. And those ads keep getting pricier. Meta says its average price per ad went up twelve percent in one year.
Because Dave was not alone. Thousands of other stores were bidding for the same eyeballs. Some of them were selling the exact same lamp.
At the end of the month, Dave opened his ad bill. And suddenly, the number on his phone made sense.
Here's the answer to the guess. Out of every hundred people who clicked, two bought a lamp. Just two.
So to sell one lamp, Dave needed fifty clicks. Fifty clicks, at fifty cents each. Twenty five dollars of ads, to sell one thirty dollar lamp.
Remember his sixteen dollars and eighty cents? Take away twenty five. Dave loses about eight dollars every time he makes a sale.
It's like a lemonade stand that pays every customer to walk over. The line looks amazing. The cash box is empty.
Over the whole month, Dave sold one hundred lamps. Three thousand dollars in sales. And two thousand five hundred dollars in ads.
Add the lamps, the fees and the plan, and Dave was already down eight hundred fifty six dollars.
Which raised a bigger question. If Dave lost money on every lamp, who exactly made money from his store?
So Dave cut his three thousand dollars into a pie, and followed every slice.
The biggest slice, two thousand five hundred dollars, went to ads. Meta made fifty nine billion dollars from ads in just three months of twenty twenty six.
Another slice went to Shopify. The monthly plan, plus a fee on every sale. Shopify's payments side brought in two point seven eight billion dollars in a single quarter.
And the supplier? Paid for every lamp, up front, before the lamp even left the factory.
Notice something? Every one of them got paid whether Dave's store won or lost. Dave was the only one taking the risk.
There's an old saying. In a gold rush, the people who get rich are the ones selling shovels. Dave thought he was the gold miner. He was the shovel customer.
That's not a crime. That's just how the business works. But Dave's month wasn't over yet. Because a lot of those lamps were still on a boat.
Dave's inbox filled up. Where is my lamp? The supplier's page said seven to twenty days. Some took much longer.
And here's a rule Dave had never heard of. In the U S, the FTC says if a seller doesn't promise a shipping time, it has to ship within thirty days. If it can't, the customer can get every cent back.
Some customers didn't even email. They called their card company and filed a chargeback. Dave lost two of those. Each one cost him the thirty dollars, plus a fifteen dollar fee.
Then came the returns. Retailers expected about one in five online purchases to be sent back last year. That's from the National Retail Federation.
Dave got twenty refund requests. But mailing a lamp back overseas cost more than the lamp. So Dave refunded the thirty dollars, and the customers just kept the lamps.
And when you refund a sale, Shopify keeps its original card fee. It's like returning a pizza and still paying the delivery guy.
Dave's final damage for the month? One thousand five hundred forty six dollars. On three thousand dollars of sales.
So Dave had a new plan. If a hundred sales lost money, he would just sell a thousand. More ads. Scale up!
Dave thought more sales would fix it. Nope. More sales made it worse.
If every lamp loses eight dollars, a thousand lamps lose eight thousand. Scaling a loss is like fixing a leaky bucket by pouring water in faster.
This was Dave's lowest moment. Savings gone. Credit card out. His thumb hovering over a big blue button that said, increase budget.
But before he pressed it, Dave found his old napkin. Because one number on it could have saved him the whole month.
Remember, this is education, not advice. Dave turned off the ads, and did the math the video never showed him.
Step one. He searched for his own product. Same glowing cat lamp, on a big shopping app. Nine dollars, shipped.
If customers can buy it cheaper in two taps, Dave isn't adding anything. Except a markup, and a very long wait.
Step two. Test tiny, with a stop rule. Fifty dollars of ads, not five hundred. If the fifty dollars doesn't come back as profit, stop.
Step three. Read the bank account, not the sales screen. Sales are the whole pizza. Profit is the slice you actually get to eat.
And the one number Dave should have checked first? Sixteen dollars and eighty cents.
That's thirty dollars, minus the twelve dollar lamp, minus the fee. It's the most Dave could pay to win one customer and still break even. Before a single refund.
Dave was paying twenty five. He was losing money before he sold his first lamp. One line of math. Thirty seconds. One thousand five hundred forty six dollars.
So Dave did not press the button. He closed the store. And month two's loss? It never happened.
Some people do build real businesses online. Usually with something that's hard to copy. Their own product, their own skill. Not the same lamp as ten thousand other stores.
Sales are not profit. Count every cost.
Know your ad ceiling before you buy a single click.
In a gold rush, the shovel sellers get paid first.
Next time, Dave's brother asks to borrow some money. Just until Friday. Dave says yes. That's the problem.

youtube.hook: Dave's dropshipping store made $3,000 in sales in its first month. His bank account went down $1,546. We follow every dollar of a $30 lamp: the payment fee, the supplier, the ads, the refunds and the chargebacks, and the one number Dave should have checked first.
